claims.text: Premelting and melting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are primarily governed by segregation of low-surface-energy, low-melting-point elements to the surface.
Surface segregation creates a liquid-like, structurally disordered shell.
The segregated shell lowers the nanoparticle's effective melting point relative to a uniformly mixed material.
The proposed starting particles are near-equimolar, single-phase, homogeneously mixed solid solutions.
Slow annealing promotes equilibrium surface segregation, whereas rapid quenching preserves a uniform elemental distribution.
Particles in the 3–10 nm range have a sufficiently high surface-to-volume ratio for the proposed surface-controlled behavior.
Relevant premelting and melting behavior should occur on heating toward or beyond approximately 70–90% of the reported bulk melting temperature.
The surface layer becomes enriched in elements with lower melting points and lower cohesive energies than the particle interior.
Minimization of overall surface free energy drives selective migration of the low-melting constituents to the surface.
The compositionally segregated shell has a reduced melting temperature.
Melting of the segregated shell nucleates and accelerates melting of the overall nanoparticle.
Slow-annealed particles will have a lower premelting onset temperature than rapidly quenched particles.
Slow-annealed particles will develop a thicker liquid-like surface layer than rapidly quenched particles.
Particles with uniform surface composition should conform more closely to classical Gibbs–Thomson melting-point predictions.
Rapidly quenched particles with minimal segregation provide a baseline governed solely by size-dependent melting-point depression.
The mechanism should apply primarily to near-equimolar, highly mixed particles smaller than about 10 nm.
The mechanism may not apply to larger particles or to alloys lacking substantial surface-energy disparities among their constituents.
The cited AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles progressively phase-separated during heating through segregation of Au and Cu to their surfaces.
XPS or atom-probe tomography can verify that the comparison groups have different surface compositions, while in situ TEM and DSC can measure the relevant melting response.
A verified surface-composition difference accompanied by no significant difference in premelting onset or premelt-layer thickness would falsify the proposed governing role of surface segregation.
